text: A user account signs in successfully from the United States, then nineteen minutes later signs in successfully again from a country on the other side of the world. No commercial flight makes that trip that fast. That pattern is called impossible travel, and it's a classic sign of a stolen credential being used from two places at once. This lesson builds a real custom analytics rule in Sentinel that catches exactly this pattern, from a blank query to a working detection.

The base query joins SigninLogs to itself on UserPrincipalName, using the join syntax from Chapter 2. ResultType equals zero keeps only successful sign-ins on both sides of the join — a failed attempt from a second country proves nothing. Extend pulls the country out of the nested LocationDetails field, and the final where clauses keep only pairs from different countries inside a one-hour window.

A query sitting in Logs only answers once. Wrapping it in a scheduled analytics rule makes it run automatically. Three settings matter here: run the query every hour, matching its own time window; look up the last hour of raw data; and set the alert threshold to trigger on any result greater than zero, since even one matching pair deserves a look.

A bare alert saying a query matched isn't enough for the investigation graph to use. Entity mapping tags UserPrincipalName as the Account entity, and both IPAddress columns as IP address entities — two separate entries, one per sign-in location. Once that's saved, any future alert touching this same account or either address links back to this one automatically.

That's a complete custom analytics rule, built the same way any real Sentinel rule gets built: a self-join query written in KQL, a schedule and alert threshold that turn it into something that runs on its own, and entity mapping tying its results into Sentinel's correlation engine. The next lesson picks up the moment this exact rule fires — working the incident it creates from the queue all the way through the investigation graph.
